title: The Science of Reading in High School: Engaging Rhetorical Exemplars in the ELA Classroom
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: This article demonstrates how Science of Reading principles — specifically, close reading, vocabulary instruction, and evidence-based argumentation — can be applied to high school ELA through the pairing of two seminal rhetorical texts: Gandhi's 'Letter to Viceroy, Lord Irwin' and Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'Letter from Birmingham Jail.' The author, a former high school teacher, describes a complete instructional sequence: initial close reading with summary paragraph development, followed by a jigsaw activity analyzing rhetorical devices across six categories, then collaborative sharing, and finally independent argumentative writing applying the rhetorical moves students have analyzed. The article makes the case that rhetoric — the traditional art of argumentation — is an underemphasized skill in contemporary education, and that careful analysis of exemplary rhetorical texts is the most effective path to developing it. The Gandhi-King pairing is particularly pedagogically powerful because Gandhi's letter preceded and influenced King's, allowing teachers to trace the lineage of argument across historical and geographic contexts. The article is practical throughout, including specific classroom protocols and a rhetorical analysis chart students can use.
points: Pairing Gandhi and King as rhetorical exemplars is not merely thematic (both nonviolent direct action) but intellectual: King was directly influenced by Gandhi, allowing students to trace how a specific argumentative tradition was adopted and adapted.

The jigsaw protocol for rhetorical analysis — individual identification of devices, collaborative chart completion, whole-class sharing — builds both individual accountability and collective knowledge construction.

The article demonstrates that Science of Reading principles apply in high school ELA not just through foundational decoding work but through explicit instruction in academic vocabulary, text structure, and evidenced argumentation.

Teaching students to identify and name specific rhetorical devices (not just 'the author uses persuasive language') gives them a vocabulary for analysis that transfers across texts, disciplines, and their own writing.
The sequence from close reading to device analysis to independent argumentative writing is a disciplinary literacy model: students read as apprentice rhetoricians before they write as emerging ones.
quotes: In contemporary public discourse, it’s clear that many people have not been taught how to argue effectively. Name-calling, groundless accusations, guilt by association, and other logical fallacies are sprinkled throughout the news, social media, and conversations.

Each semester, I thought of this unit as my small attempt to address this broader problem by at least introducing the students in my class to a better way. The core of the unit was the pairing of two seminal rhetorical texts: “Letter to Viceroy, Lord Irwin” by Mohandas Gandhi [ ] and “Letter from a Birmingham Jail” by Dr.

I would begin the unit with Gandhi’s letter, since it preceded King and served as an inspiration for his nonviolent direct action during the Civil Rights Movement. After guiding my students through a close reading of the text and developing a summary paragraph, I would direct their attention to the rhetorical devices for a second look at the text using a jigsaw activity.

Following this, I would call on members from each group to share an example of each rhetorical device, and I would restate and clarify the way each example demonstrated an effective use of rhetoric. Lastly, after our whole class discussion, students would complete a SOAPSTone analysis chart and paragraph to synthesize their thinking about Gandhi’s message and his use of rhetoric.

First, given the length of the letter, I would strategically scaffold the reading of the text. To start, I would set our expectations and direct students to look for and annotate certain elements in King’s prose.

Finally, I would have students write a gist or summary statement for the first eleven paragraphs. This prepares students to engage in a similar routine that they will complete in groups as we jigsawed the remaining paragraphs of the letter.

Lastly, one element of their assessment over this unit was a written comparison of the use of rhetoric in the two texts. This assignment helps students demonstrate their analysis and argumentation skills, their ability to cite and interpret text evidence, and practice synthesizing information from two separate sources.
